title: Single Number III
description: Brute force to optimized: a hash map versus XOR combined with a bit based grouping split.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer array nums where exactly two elements appear only once and every other element appears exactly twice, find the two elements that appear only once, in any order.

blocks.caption: Input flows through XOR-all-then-split-by-a-differing-bit to reveal both singles

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums where exactly two elements appear only once and every other element appears exactly twice, find the two elements that appear only once, in any order.

blocks.title: Analogy: Two Unpaired Socks in a Laundry Basket
blocks.text: Like the single unpaired sock problem, but this time exactly two socks are missing their partners instead of just one, requiring a way to tell the two lone socks apart from each other as well as from the paired ones.

blocks.caption: XOR everything, then use one differing bit to split into two groups, each canceling down to one single value

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["1 and 2 each appear twice, 3 and 5 each appear once","3 and 5 are the two singles","Every value that appears exactly twice contributes nothing once XOR cancellation is applied, leaving only the two singles as candidates"],["Answer","[3, 5] (in any order)","The problem does not require a specific order between the two returned values"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Both values appear only once, with nothing else in the array","both are singles","With no duplicates present at all, every value in the array is by definition one of the two singles being searched for"],["Answer","[-1, 0] (in any order)","Two's complement makes -1 and 0 behave identically to any other integers under XOR"]]}

blocks.text: With exactly two elements and no repeats at all, both are trivially the two singles being searched for, [1, 0] or [0, 1] (order does not matter).

The 'find the one value that appears once' version of this problem is solved by XORing everything together, since every paired value cancels out. Here there are two unknowns instead of one, so it helps to ask what happens when that same trick is applied directly.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: XORing the entire array together does not reveal either single value directly, since it produces the XOR of the two singles combined, not each one individually.

Observation 2: That combined XOR value cannot be zero, because the two singles are guaranteed to be different from each other, so at least one bit position must differ between them.

Observation 3: Any bit position where they differ can be used to split every number in the array into two groups, and crucially, every paired value has identical bits in both copies, so both copies of any pair always land in the same group together.

Observation 4: That means each group contains exactly one of the two singles plus a complete set of intact pairs, so XORing within each group separately cancels its pairs and leaves that group's one single value behind.

So instead of solving for two unknowns at once, the differing bit lets the array be split into two independent 'exactly one unknown' subproblems, each solvable with the same trick that works for one single value.
This split-by-a-differing-bit idea is exactly what separates the brute force hash map approach below from the optimized solution.
Count every value's frequency using a hash map built in one pass, then collect the two values whose count is exactly 1.

items: Build a frequency count for every value in the array.
Collect every value whose count is exactly 1.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Building a full frequency count first guarantees every value's true occurrence count is known before any values are collected, avoiding any risk of missing a single.
Filtering for count equal to 1 after the full pass is complete directly matches the problem's definition of the values being searched for.
This approach works for any number of single values, not just exactly two, though it uses more memory than the structure of this specific problem requires.

blocks.text: Every value's true count is directly computed, so both single values are correctly found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to count, one pass over the distinct values.
Space: O(n), for the frequency map in the worst case.

Limitation: a hash map uses more memory than necessary, when the same "everything paired except some exceptions" structure that made simple XOR work for one single value can be extended, with one extra clever step, to handle exactly two single values in O(1) extra space.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why brute force is limited: it needs a hash map sized to the number of distinct values, using O(n) extra space when the structure of this specific problem allows much less.

What it wastes: it tracks an exact count for every value, when only the two singles actually need to be found.

Can we avoid the wasted work: yes. XORing the whole array cancels every pair automatically, though this alone only produces the combined XOR of the two singles, not each one separately.

Can the results combine into one step: yes. Using any bit where that combined XOR is 1 to split the array into two groups turns "find two singles" into two independent "find one single" subproblems, each solvable with a plain XOR pass.

XOR every element of the array together. Every paired value cancels out, leaving exactly the XOR of the two single values. Since the two single values are different from each other, this combined XOR is guaranteed to have at least one set bit, a position where the two singles differ. Using that one differing bit to split every number in the array into two groups (based on whether they have that bit set), each group ends up containing one of the two singles plus a complete set of pairs (since every paired value has identical bits, both copies always land in the same group), so XORing within each group in isolation cancels the pairs and reveals that group's single value.
XOR everything to find a differing bit, then split into two groups using that bit and XOR each group separately.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["XOR every element together","1 xor 2 xor 1 xor 3 xor 2 xor 5 = 3 xor 5 = 6 (binary 110)","Every paired value (1 and 2) cancels out in the running XOR, leaving only the XOR of the two singles, 3 and 5"],["Pick the lowest set bit of 6 (bit 1, value 2)","this bit differs between the two singles","Since 6 is nonzero, at least one bit must be set, and any set bit is guaranteed to differ between 3 and 5"],["Group A: numbers with bit 1 set (2, 3, 2)","XOR within group A: 2 xor 3 xor 2 = 3","Both copies of 2 share bit 1 and land together in this group, so they cancel, leaving only the single value 3"],["Group B: numbers with bit 1 not set (1, 1, 5)","XOR within group B: 1 xor 1 xor 5 = 5","Both copies of 1 share the same bit pattern and land together here too, canceling and leaving only the single value 5"],["Answer","[3, 5]","Each group's leftover XOR is exactly one of the two original single values"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: split into two groups using a differing bit, XOR each group to reveal one single each

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a constant number of passes over the array.
Space: O(1), only a handful of running values are kept.

The full-array XOR cancels every paired value, since XORing any value with itself is 0, leaving only the XOR of the two unknown singles. That combined value must be nonzero because the two singles are different, and any bit where it is 1 marks a position where the two singles disagree. Splitting the array on that bit is safe precisely because a pair's two identical copies always share the same bit pattern, so they are guaranteed to fall into the same group and cancel there, leaving each group holding exactly one clean single value.

items: xorAll accumulates the XOR of the entire array in one pass, which collapses to just the XOR of the two singles since every pair cancels.
xorAll AND negative xorAll isolates only the lowest set bit of xorAll, a simple and reliable way to grab any one bit where the two singles are known to differ.
The second pass routes each number into groupA or groupB based on that one bit, and XORing within each group separately reveals that group's single value once its pairs cancel out.

blocks.text: The key insight extending single number XOR cancellation to two unknowns is that any bit where the two singles differ can be used to partition the whole array so that every pair stays together in the same group, guaranteeing each group cancels down to exactly one of the two answers.

items: Forgetting that any differing bit works for the split, not just the lowest one, though the lowest set bit is the simplest to isolate using x AND negative x.
Assuming a single overall XOR pass alone can separate two unknown values without the grouping step, which is not possible without first splitting into two independent groups.
Trying to figure out ahead of time which single belongs in which group, when the whole point of the bit-based split is that it works correctly without knowing either single value in advance.

items: Draw the grouping step explicitly: show why every paired value, having identical bits, always lands in the same group together, which is the detail that makes the whole trick provably correct.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If they say "can you do this in O(1) space", think about reusing the same XOR cancellation trick that works for a single unknown, applied twice via a grouping split.
If they ask "what if there were three or more single values instead of two", think about why the clean bit-based split argument breaks down beyond two unknowns.
If they ask "why does the grouping never separate a pair", think about why two identical numbers always share every bit, including the one chosen for splitting.

items: What if the array had exactly one single value instead of two? How would the solution simplify?
Why does this bit-based grouping approach not extend cleanly to three or more single values?
Could you solve this using a hash set instead of full frequency counting, and would that improve the brute force?
How would you verify, without extra data structures, that your two answers are correct?

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (XOR plus bit based grouping): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: XOR cancellation extended with a bit-based grouping split
Core Idea: XOR the whole array to get the combined XOR of the two singles, then split on any bit where they differ so each group cancels down to one single
Time: O(n) for both approaches
Space: O(1) for the optimized solution, O(n) for brute force
Most Important Observation: any bit where the combined XOR is set is guaranteed to separate the two singles into different groups without ever splitting a pair
Interview Difficulty: Intermediate, a natural follow-up once Single Number is understood
One-line memory trick: XOR reveals the combined difference, then a differing bit turns two unknowns into two separate one-unknown problems
